Medical Neuroanatomy · Chapter 3 · Case 3-1

Progressive Weakness with Mixed Upper and Lower Motor Neuron Signs

68-year-old man, 9 months of progressive limb weakness, atrophy, and bulbar involvement, with a completely normal sensory exam — worked up as motor neuron disease (ALS).

Text 100%
Localization Finding Term Pattern Workup / Trajectory

Chief Complaint

This 68-year-old, left-handed, retired businessman is complaining of progressive weakness and atrophy of his extremity musculature1.

History of Chief Complaint

He has enjoyed good health up until 9 months prior to the current presentation. At that time the patient had noticed an abnormal weakness in his arms; over the 9-month period since, the weakness has become progressively worse, spreading to his legs2. He also commented that his hands had become much thinner than before3. Three months prior to his current evaluation, his wife noted a change in his speech; in addition, he began to have difficulty swallowing4. Recently, he has experienced difficulty dressing and eating. At present, he no longer feels capable of safely driving the family car.

Family History

He is married, his wife is alive and they have two children, both of whom are no longer residing in the house.

Medical History

Tonsillectomy at age 12 and a hernia repair operation at age 455.

General Physical Examination

He is an awake, oriented, well-hydrated man who appears slightly older than his stated age and of lean habitus. Pharynx was non-reddened and no cervical lymphadenopathy was present. His heart rate was 78 and blood pressure was 125/83; respirations were 18. Peripheral pulses were intact at the wrists and ankles6. Abdomen was soft with no masses; normal bowel sounds were present. Extremities were four in number. Significant loss of muscle mass was noticeable in the shoulders, arms, and less so in the legs. Muscle loss was most prominent in the thenar eminence of both hands7.

Neurologic Examination

Mental Status

He was awake and oriented for time and place. His fund of knowledge and memory were appropriate for his age. He could recite a list of the last five presidents and accurately follow four-step commands8. His speech was slow and his pronunciation of words was slurred; however, speech patterns and content were meaningful9. He gave an accurate history.

Cranial Nerves

His visual fields were full and he had a complete range of eye movements. Pupillary reflexes were intact to both direct and consensual light. Facial expressions were intact and bilaterally symmetrical; the corneal, jaw-jerk, and gag reflexes were trace10. He reported that touching the corneal surface hurt. His tongue protruded on the midline, but was weak; fasciculations were present on the surface of the tongue11. Response to pinprick was intact throughout his face12.

Motor Systems

Strength was 3/5 at the shoulder and elbow and 2/5 at the wrist bilaterally; grip strength was 2/513. Strength was 3/5 at the hip, knee and ankle bilaterally. Deep tendon reflexes were elevated at 3/4 around the knees and 4/4 around the ankles14. Deep tendon reflexes were depressed at the elbows and wrists (1/4)15. Significant atrophy was present bilaterally in the forearms and arms and most prominent in the thenar eminences16. Widespread fasciculations were noted at rest in all four extremities17. The patient was able to rise from a chair and walk only a short distance unassisted. A fine tremor was present in the upper extremities when they were held in the extended and pronated position. The tremor diminished when his arms were lowered into a resting position18. He noted that the tremor becomes worse when he is feeling stressed and when he drinks 2-3 cups of coffee. Finger-to-nose and heel-to-shin testing was normal in all extremities. No pronator drift was observed19. His bowel and bladder functions were intact20.

Sensory Exam

Discriminative touch, vibratory sense, proprioception, and pain and temperature sensation were intact throughout his body21.

Follow-Up

Re-examination in six months revealed strength at the shoulder and elbow to be 2/5 and at the wrist 1/5. Grip strength was also 1/522. Strength at the hip was 3/5 and at the knee and ankle 2/5. Deep tendon reflexes remained trace to 1/4 in the upper extremity, 2/4 at the knee and 1/4 at the ankle23. He lacked any gag response and complained of frequent episodes of choking when swallowing24.

Questions

  1. Has the patient experienced any changes in consciousness or cognition, language function or spatial recognition, personality or emotional behavior, or any loss in memory?
  2. Does the patient exhibit any loss of vision and if so, where in the visual field is the loss? Are there any visual hallucinations present in this patient?
  3. Are there any changes in cranial nerve function and if so, are they signs of suprasegmental or segmental level defects?
  4. Are there any changes in motor function such as reflexes, muscle tone, movement, or coordination, and if so, are they signs of suprasegmental or segmental level defects?
  5. Are there any changes in sensory function and if so, what levels of the body have experienced this change?
  6. What is the clinical temporal profile of this patient's neurologic problem: is the onset of neurologic findings acute or insidious? Is the course chronically progressive, fluctuant, or stable?
  7. Based on the presenting signs and symptoms, do you think the distribution of the neurologic pathology is focal, multifocal, or diffuse?
  8. Based on the answers to these questions, develop a differential diagnosis of the patient's neurological problem.
  9. If the origin of the pathology is vascular, what arterial supply is most likely involved with the lesion in this patient?

Clinical Reasoning Walkthrough

From exam to diagnosis

01 · Localization

The motor neurons themselves — both orders

The arms show lower motor neuron (LMN) signs — atrophy, fasciculations, and hyporeflexia. The legs show upper motor neuron (UMN) signs — hyperreflexia. The bulbar exam shows LMN signs too (tongue atrophy and fasciculations). None of this can be explained by a single lesion in one tract or one level — it localizes to the motor neurons themselves, at multiple levels, sparing every sensory pathway completely.

02 · Distribution

Diffuse / multifocal, not focal

This isn't confined to one myotome, one root, one nerve, or one plexus. It spans bulbar muscles (tongue), both arms, and both legs — a diffuse, roughly symmetric process, which is itself a major clue against a single structural or compressive lesion.

03 · Time Course

Insidious onset, chronically progressive

Symptoms crept in gradually over 9 months and kept worsening at every re-check, with no fluctuation or plateau. That combination — insidious onset plus relentless progression, not an acute event and not a fluctuating course — argues against trauma, stroke, and fatigable neuromuscular junction disease alike.

04 · Differential Diagnosis

ALS is a diagnosis of exclusion — there's no single confirmatory test. You work through the mimics that could produce part of this picture, and rule each one out on a specific detail, until motor neuron disease is the only explanation left standing.

DiagnosisFitsArgues against
ALS / motor neuron diseaseMost likely Mixed UMN (legs, hyperreflexia) + LMN (arms, bulbar: atrophy, fasciculations, hyporeflexia) signs; completely normal sensory exam; chronic, relentless progression over months —
Cervical stenosis / spondylotic myelopathy Can produce a similar "LMN at the lesion, UMN below it" split (root compression + cord compression) Wouldn't produce fasciculations, doesn't explain tongue involvement, and no sensory level or bowel/bladder change even at 6 months
Traumatic spinal cord injury Can produce a mixed UMN/LMN picture depending on the level and extent of injury No antecedent trauma in the history, and trauma presents acutely — not as an insidious, 9-month progressive course
Myasthenia gravis Bulbar symptoms (dysphagia, dysarthria) can occur No fatigability or fluctuation described; atrophy, fasciculations, and hyperreflexia are not features of a pure neuromuscular junction disease
Multifocal motor neuropathy Pure motor, progressive distal weakness Typically asymmetric and conduction-block driven; doesn't produce UMN signs (hyperreflexia) or bulbar involvement
Syringomyelia (cervical) Can cause LMN arm signs plus UMN leg signs from a central cord lesion Classically causes a dissociated cape-like loss of pain/temperature at the level — this patient's sensory exam is entirely normal

05 · Diagnostic Workup

  1. EMG / nerve conduction studiesLook for widespread denervation (fibrillations, fasciculation potentials, reduced recruitment) in multiple limbs and bulbar muscles, with normal sensory nerve conduction studies — the electrophysiologic signature of motor neuron disease.
  2. MRI brain and cervical spineRule out a structural mimic — cervical spondylotic myelopathy, foramen magnum lesion, or a structural brainstem process — before accepting a neurodegenerative diagnosis.
  3. LabsB12, TSH, CK, and (if a demyelinating motor neuropathy is on the table) anti-GM1 antibodies — reversible or alternative causes should be excluded.
  4. Pulmonary function testingForced vital capacity, given the bulbar involvement and the respiratory risk that comes with progressive motor neuron disease.
  5. Swallow evaluationFormal assessment given the documented dysphagia and choking episodes — aspiration risk needs to be quantified early.
  6. Neurology / ALS clinic referralFor diagnostic confirmation, genetic counseling if family history emerges, and multidisciplinary care planning.

06 · Prognosis

ALS is relentlessly progressive; average survival is roughly 2-5 years from diagnosis, though this varies widely. Bulbar-onset involvement — present here just three months into the disease — is generally associated with faster progression and higher aspiration/respiratory risk than limb-onset disease alone.

07 · Management

  • Riluzole or edaravone (disease-modifying agents with a modest survival benefit)
  • Multidisciplinary ALS clinic: PT/OT, speech-language pathology, dietitian, respiratory therapy
  • Non-invasive ventilation as respiratory function declines
  • PEG tube consideration given documented dysphagia and aspiration risk
  • Symptom management: cramps/fasciculation discomfort, sialorrhea, pseudobulbar affect if present
  • Early goals-of-care and advance care planning conversations, given the prognosis

Concept Deep-Dive

The neuroanatomy behind the exam

click any image to enlarge

Localization

Mixed UMN + LMN at a glance

The whole case in one picture: spasticity/hyperreflexia/Babinski (UMN) on one side of the diagram, flaccid weakness/atrophy/fasciculations/tongue atrophy (LMN) on the other, and the shared pathophysiology — degeneration of both neuron orders — on the right.

Side by side: this patient's legs match the top row, his arms and tongue match the bottom row — at the same visit.

Most spinal cord lesions give you one pattern or the other, not both at once. Getting a clean UMN picture in one region and a clean LMN picture in another, with sensation completely untouched, is exactly what should make you think "motor neuron disease" rather than "one lesion, one place."

Pattern

ALS clinical features, all in one reference

A full-body reference sheet — worth keeping open alongside the case while you work through the exam findings below.

One box on this chart is worth calling out specifically: cognitive/behavioral association. A meaningful minority of ALS patients develop frontotemporal dysfunction — the ALS-FTD spectrum — with behavioral or executive changes. This patient's mental status exam is explicitly normal (he recited five presidents and followed four-step commands without difficulty), so nothing here suggests that's happening in his case, but it's a real part of the disease spectrum worth knowing exists.

Notice how closely the "sensory and sphincter findings" and "diagnostic clues" boxes match this patient's actual exam — preserved sensation, no early bladder involvement, and a diagnosis built from the combination and spread of UMN+LMN signs rather than any single confirmatory test.

Finding

Ventral horn damage: where the LMN signs come from

The ventral (anterior) gray horn houses the alpha motor neuron cell bodies — the lower motor neurons for skeletal muscle.

The ventral horn is where lower motor neuron cell bodies actually live. When they degenerate — whether from ALS, polio, or any anterior horn cell disease — the muscles they used to command lose their nerve supply entirely. Denervated muscle doesn't just weaken: it loses its normal trophic support, atrophies, and becomes electrically unstable, which is what produces fasciculations (spontaneous, visible twitches too weak to move the joint) and fibrillations (seen only on EMG).

This patient's arm and tongue findings — atrophy, fasciculations, hyporeflexia — are the textbook signature of ventral horn (and, for the tongue, cranial nerve XII nucleus) cell loss, not a problem with the nerve, muscle, or neuromuscular junction downstream.

Localization

Corticospinal tract: where the leg's UMN signs come from

The corticospinal tract runs from motor cortex, crosses at the pyramidal decussation, and finally synapses on the ventral horn cells it commands.

The lateral corticospinal tract (boxed) is the upper motor neuron's cable — separate from the ventral horn cell bodies it terminates on.

In ALS, upper motor neurons in the motor cortex and lower motor neurons in the brainstem/spinal cord degenerate independently — not necessarily at the same rate, and not necessarily in the same body region at the same time. When corticospinal input to a segment is lost before the ventral horn cells themselves die, that segment shows hyperreflexia and spasticity (UMN signs) — which is exactly this patient's leg picture, months before the same process catches up to the ventral horn cells there too.

Both neuron orders are dying in this disease — they're just doing it on different timelines in different regions, which is why one limb can look UMN and another can look LMN in the very same patient.

Term

Why “amyotrophic lateral sclerosis” is a bit of a misnomer

Both colors in this key die in ALS — that's the whole disease in one picture.

The real evidence behind the old "sclerosis" name: (b) the lateral corticospinal tract lights up on MRI (yellow) against normal white matter (red); (c–h) it stains differently on histology and immunohistochemistry too — this is what pathologists were originally seeing on that gliotic patch.

The name comes from 19th-century postmortem histology: pathologists found pale, gliotic patches where the lateral corticospinal tract should have been, and assumed the disease started as fibrosis or "sclerosis" building up in the lateral columns of the cord. That's backwards. ALS isn't a demyelinating or fibrotic disease — it's a disease of neuronal cell body death, and the sclerosis on those old slides was a downstream consequence of axons dying back after their parent cell bodies were already gone.

The neurons that die are specifically the largest cell bodies in the motor system: Betz cells (giant pyramidal neurons in the motor cortex — the upper motor neuron's own cell body) and alpha motor neurons in the spinal cord's ventral horn (the lower motor neuron's cell body). Both populations degenerate in this disease — just not necessarily at the same rate, in the same place, at the same time.

That mismatched rate is exactly why this patient's legs currently read as UMN (Betz cell loss outpacing ventral horn loss there) while his arms read as LMN (the reverse) — two expressions of the same underlying cell-death process, just imbalanced by region.

Finding

The corticobulbar tract: why the bulbar signs are mixed too

The corticobulbar tract (upper motor neuron) synapses on the motor nuclei of the cranial nerves — the bulbar lower motor neurons living in the pons and medulla.

The same UMN/LMN logic playing out in the limbs plays out in the face and throat. The corticobulbar tract carries upper motor neuron input down to the motor nuclei of the cranial nerves — the bulbar lower motor neurons that directly command the tongue (hypoglossal nucleus, CN XII), palate and pharynx (nucleus ambiguus, CN IX/X), and jaw (trigeminal motor nucleus, CN V).

This patient's tongue fasciculations and weakness are an LMN sign at the hypoglossal nucleus itself. His merely trace jaw-jerk and gag reflexes sit in between fully brisk (pure UMN) and fully absent (pure LMN) — because both the corticobulbar input above and the brainstem motor nuclei themselves are being lost together, just as in the limbs. This combined limb-plus-bulbar pattern is one of the more common ALS presentations, and it's exactly what unfolded here three months after the arm weakness began.

Finding

The split-hand sign: why the thumb side goes first

Panel A: the three leading hypotheses for how ALS spreads at all — dying forward (cortex to cord), dying back (muscle/NMJ inward), or independent degeneration. Panels B–E: why the thenar side (APB) wastes before the hypothenar side (ADM) even within the same hand.

This patient's thenar-predominant wasting is a named finding: the split-hand sign, where thumb-side intrinsic muscles (like abductor pollicis brevis) waste faster than pinky-side muscles (like abductor digiti minimi), even though both are innervated by nerves exiting the same spinal segments. Nobody has definitively nailed down why, but the leading explanations converge on the same idea — the motor neurons and corticomotoneuronal connections controlling fine thumb movements are simply used harder and more precisely than those for the pinky, which may make them more metabolically vulnerable in a disease that preferentially kills busy, high-demand neurons first.

Same logic as the leg's UMN signs versus the arm's LMN signs: this disease doesn't spread evenly. It picks off the most active, most finely-tuned motor neuron populations first — whether that's comparing hand to hip, or thumb to pinky within the very same hand.

Localization

Why sensation stays completely normal

Dorsal columns and the anterolateral (spinothalamic) system are physically separate white-matter tracts from the anterior horn and corticospinal system — anatomically distinct real estate.

ALS is, by definition, a disease of motor neurons — it doesn't touch the sensory neurons whose cell bodies sit safely outside the cord in the dorsal root ganglia, or the ascending tracts (dorsal columns, spinothalamic) that carry their signals up. That's precisely why this patient's discriminative touch, vibration, proprioception, and pain/temperature are untouched at every single visit.

A completely normal sensory exam paired with widespread, progressive motor findings is one of the single most useful clues in this case — it's what lets you rule out almost every structural cord, root, and plexus lesion in one line of the exam.

Workup / Trajectory

Why arms and legs can be hit differently: the cord isn't uniform

Cervical (a), thoracic (b), and lumbar (c) cross-sections side by side — the ventral horn is a different size at every level, because it houses a different number of motor neurons for a different amount of muscle.

The cervical and lumbosacral segments are enlarged specifically because they contain far more ventral horn motor neurons — enough to command the muscles of an entire limb — while the thoracic cord (mostly trunk muscle) has a much smaller ventral horn. A disease that attacks motor neurons doesn't have to hit every pool equally or simultaneously; the size and vulnerability of a given motor neuron pool can shape which body region shows disease first and worst.

Within a given ventral horn, the spread usually follows its own pattern too: motor neurons for distal muscles (fine, precise movements — fingers, hand) tend to go first, with proximal muscles following as the disease works medially across the horn. Eventually, in advanced disease, it can reach the most medial motor neuron pools of all — the ones driving axial and respiratory muscles, which is exactly why pulmonary function monitoring is part of this patient's workup.

This is part of why a diffuse motor neuron disease can still produce a patchwork clinical picture — arms affected before legs, one hand more than the other, distal before proximal — rather than a uniform, all-at-once deficit.

Pattern

What this actually looks like under the microscope

Sacral cord, real histology — notice how little white matter surrounds the gray matter this low in the cord, compared to cervical levels.

Quick reference: every ascending and descending tract, numbered, with the somatotopic (C/T/L/S) organization used throughout this course.

The schematics used everywhere else in this note are simplifications of exactly this kind of tissue. White matter (myelinated tract fibers) surrounds a gray, H-shaped core (cell bodies) at every level, but the proportions change dramatically from level to level — more white matter relative to gray matter higher up in the cord, since cervical white matter has to carry information for the whole cord below it, while sacral white matter only carries information for the segments below the sacrum (not much).

Keeping one real histological image in view is a good check against over-schematizing — the textbook ovals and blobs really do correspond to a gray H sitting inside a white matter ring, just messier and less color-coded in real tissue.

Localization

Segmental vs. suprasegmental — this case breaks the clean split

Which pattern is present?
ARMS/BULBAR ↓LEGS ↓
Segmental (LMN)
atrophy · fasciculations · ↓reflexes
Suprasegmental (UMN)
hyperreflexia

both patterns, same patient, same visit — that combination is itself the clue

Most of this course's cases (like the hemicord stab wound) teach you to sort a patient into one box or the other. Motor neuron disease is the exception that proves the rule: it can degenerate upper and lower motor neurons at different rates in different regions, so a single patient can legitimately show both patterns at once — arms/bulbar segmental, legs suprasegmental.

Don't force this patient into one box. The fact that he doesn't fit cleanly into either is the diagnosis.

Workup / Trajectory

If it were vascular: answering the case's own Question 9

Anterior spinal artery (supplies the ventral horns and corticospinal tracts bilaterally) vs. paired posterior spinal arteries (dorsal columns).

The case explicitly asks which vessel would be responsible if this were vascular. An anterior spinal artery occlusion would fit the motor picture reasonably well — it supplies the ventral horns and corticospinal tracts on both sides — but it would also produce bilateral pain/temperature loss (it carries the spinothalamic tracts too) and, critically, would present acutely, not over 9 insidious months.

This patient's normal sensory exam and slow, progressive time course both argue against a vascular explanation — but knowing why is exactly what the question is testing.
